implementation_notes: The .NET realization is Monitor.TryEnter, which attempts the lock and reports the outcome through the lockTaken reference instead of blocking; the state check runs inside the same monitor region and the exit belongs in a finally block guarded by lockTaken. lock/Monitor.Enter always block and therefore cannot balk, so the Try* family is the essential primitive: Monitor.TryEnter, SemaphoreSlim.Wait(0), ChannelWriter.TryWrite and the TryAdd/TryDequeue methods of the concurrent collections, with Interlocked.CompareExchange covering the lock-free state transition. Asynchronous methods cannot hold a monitor across await, so there the balking decision moves to a SemaphoreSlim(1,1) probed with Wait(0) or to an asynchronous channel.
pitfalls: Monitor.TryEnter(obj, timeout) with a nonzero timeout waits for the lock - 'right now' semantics require 0 (or the TryEnter(obj) overload).
Monitor.Exit must run exactly when lockTaken became true; releasing on a failed attempt (or not releasing on a successful one) corrupts the monitor.
A monitor cannot span await, so an asynchronous guarded method must use SemaphoreSlim.Wait(0) or a channel instead of Monitor.
